docs.title: nodestrength
docs.text:
Node strength and hemispheric asymmetry analysis for diffusion MRI connectomes.

nodestrength takes a square structural connectome (the output of tractography + tck2connectome) and computes:

  1. Per-region connectivity strength (Brain Connectivity Toolbox strengths_und)
  2. Left–right asymmetry indices (side, SOZ-aligned, log-ratio, intrahemispheric)
  3. Optional ROI volume and volume AI
  4. Optional normative z-scores and mixed-design GLMs
  5. Optional one-page clinical PDF reports

It implements the analysis layer of Piper et al., Epilepsia (2026)1, and is atlas-agnostic. Built-in grids are Lausanne + THOMAS (the paper) and MRtrix3 fs_default Desikan–Killiany (84 nodes).

This site is modelled on the layout of QSIPrep: installation, data, CLI, outputs, then the science. The Science section is a reading path for people new to networks, connectomics, and graph theory in neuroscience, with citations into the literature.

Author: Philbert Ndagijimana · Contact: phindagijimana@gmail.com · Source: github.com/phindagijimana/dwi-AI

docs.title: What it is — and is not
docs.text:
This tool Not this tool Analysis of already built connectomes A replacement for QSIPrep / QSIRecon Weighted node strength + laterality Full BCT catalogue (clustering, efficiency, modularity, …) Structural (dMRI) graphs fMRI functional connectivity pipelines Applied network neuroscience Abstract graph-theory theorems

QSIPrep preprocesses dMRI; QSIRecon reconstructs FODs and connectomes; nodestrength scores those connectomes.

flowchart LR
  BIDS[BIDS dMRI] --> QSIPrep
  QSIPrep --> QSIRecon
  QSIRecon --> C[connectome.csv]
  C --> NS[nodestrength]
  NS --> S[strength + AI + reports]

docs.title: A minimal command
docs.text:
DK / DKT connectomes from QSIRecon labelconvert (one folder per subject, dkt_connectome.csv):

dkt-ai-cohort \
    --root /path/to/dkt_connectomes \
    --out  /path/to/node_strength_results \
    --with-volume-ai

IDEAS-style preprocessed archive:

nodestrength inspect /path/to/ideas_ii
nodestrength ingest-preprocessed --archive /path/to/archive --out cohort.csv
nodestrength asymmetry --cohort cohort.csv --out ai.csv

See Running and the command-line reference.

docs.title: About this project
docs.text:
nodestrength is a Python analysis layer for already reconstructed structural connectomes. It implements the node-strength and laterality design of Piper et al., Epilepsia (2026)1, and is maintained by Philbert Ndagijimana.

  • Author: Philbert Ndagijimana
  • Contact: phindagijimana@gmail.com
  • Documentation: phindagijimana.github.io/dwi-AI
  • Source: github.com/phindagijimana/dwi-AI
  • Container: docker.io/phindagijimana321/nodestrength

docs.title: Scientific claim of the software
docs.text:
Given a square weighted adjacency matrix and an atlas:

  1. Compute undirected node strength (BCT strengths_und; Rubinov & Sporns 2010).
  2. Pair homologous regions and compute asymmetry indices.
  3. Optionally residualise against a control GAM and run mixed-design GLMs.

It does not claim a new graph-theoretic invariant. It claims a reproducible implementation of a published epilepsy connectomics analysis, plus a documented CLI.

docs.title: Relation to QSIPrep
docs.text: This documentation site is organised like QSIPrep’s (install → prepare data → run → CLI → outputs → pipeline) because that is how neuroimaging users already read tools. nodestrength is not QSIPrep. QSIPrep preprocesses dMRI (Cieslak et al. 2021); this package scores connectomes.

docs.title: Relation to IDEAS / Lausanne analyses
docs.text: Research scripts under research/ in the GitHub repository apply the same strength+AI maths to IDEAS I/II Lausanne connectomes (hippocampus, scales 36–250, Count/FA/Length, det vs prob). Those scripts are study-specific. They are not the public CLI. Do not commit identified clinical tables to the public repo.

docs.title: Command-line reference
docs.text:
Installed scripts: nodestrength, dkt-ai-cohort, and alias dk-ai-cohort.

This page is the QSIPrep-style flag list. Conceptual walkthrough: Running.

docs.title: nodestrength
docs.text:
nodestrength [-h]
    {run-subject,compute-strength,fit-normative,analyze,
     ingest-ideas,ingest-preprocessed,inspect,asymmetry}
    ...

-h, --help     show this help message and exit

docs.title: run-subject
docs.text:
Full FreeSurfer / THOMAS / MRtrix3 reconstruction plus analysis for one subject. Requires the reconstruction stack on PATH (or the container). For connectomes you already have, use dkt-ai-cohort or compute-strength instead.

nodestrength run-subject SUBJECT_ID \
    --t1 PATH --dwi PATH --bvec PATH --bval PATH \
    --rpe-b0 PATH \
    --subjects-dir DIR \
    --out-dir DIR \
    [--dry-run]
Flag Required Meaning SUBJECT_ID yes FreeSurfer / BIDS id --t1 yes T1w NIfTI --dwi, --bvec, --bval yes dMRI --rpe-b0 yes Reverse-phase-encode b0 --subjects-dir yes SUBJECTS_DIR --out-dir yes Derivatives --dry-run no Print planned steps only

docs.title: compute-strength
docs.text:
Per-nucleus strength and volume from an already-built connectome and a Lausanne+THOMAS lookup.

nodestrength compute-strength \
    --subject-id ID \
    --connectome PATH \
    --lookup PATH \
    --labels PATH \
    --out PATH
Flag Meaning --connectome Square MRtrix3 connectome CSV --lookup Node-lookup table (row order of the matrix) --labels Merged Lausanne+THOMAS label NIfTI (volumes) --out Output CSV

The matrix is loaded as a square numeric array; undirected strength is BCT strengths_und (via bctpy if installed).

docs.title: fit-normative
docs.text:
Fit per-(nucleus, side) OLS models on a control long-form cohort and pickle them (Piper et al. 2026 covariates: age, sex, mean ROI strength, motion; volume models use ICV).

nodestrength fit-normative --controls PATH --out PATH.pkl

docs.title: analyze
docs.text:
Mixed-design GLM: Pillai’s trace and partial η² (nodestrength.stats).

nodestrength analyze \
    --cohort PATH \
    --within nucleus side \
    --between group \
    --value strength \
    --out glm.csv \
    [--subject-col subject]
Flag Default Meaning --cohort required Long-form table --within required One or more within-subject factors --between required One or more between-subject factors --value required Outcome column --subject-col subject Subject id column --out required Result CSV

docs.title: ingest-ideas
docs.text:
Walk an IDEAS raw BIDS root and write a subject manifest.

nodestrength ingest-ideas --bids DIR --out PATH [--participants TSV] [--include ID ...]

docs.title: ingest-preprocessed
docs.text:
Build a long-form cohort from an IDEAS II pre-processed archive (skips recon-all / THOMAS / MRtrix3).

nodestrength ingest-preprocessed \
    --archive DIR \
    --out PATH \
    [--participants TSV] \
    [--include ID ...]

docs.title: inspect
docs.text:
Readiness probe: raw BIDS, pre-processed archive, or a mixed tree.

nodestrength inspect PATH [--json PATH]

Prints subjects found, ROI-name sanity, participants.tsv column map, and a single verdict: READY / PARTIAL / NOTHING_FOUND. Exit status is 0 only when the verdict starts with READY.

docs.title: asymmetry
docs.text:
Collapse a long-form cohort into per-(subject, nucleus) AI (side, SOZ-aligned, log).

nodestrength asymmetry \
    --cohort PATH \
    --out PATH \
    [--value strength] \
    [--soz-side-col soz_side]

--value can be strength or volume (or any numeric column). --soz-side-col is L/R per patient.

There is no nodestrength report subcommand. Clinical PDFs are written by dkt-ai-cohort (on by default; --no-report to skip).

docs.title: dkt-ai-cohort
docs.text:
DK / DKT (MRtrix fs_default 84-node) cohort runner.

dkt-ai-cohort --root DIR --out DIR
              [--fs-root DIR]
              [--include ID ...]
              [--with-volume-ai]
              [--report | --no-report]
              [--participants TSV]
              [--normative-model PATH.pkl]
              [--control-group control]
Argument Default Meaning --root required One folder per subject containing dkt_connectome.csv --out required node_strength_results directory (created) --fs-root none FreeSurfer SUBJECTS_DIR (find dk_nodes.mif) --include all Restrict subject IDs (sub- prefix optional) --with-volume-ai off Volumes from dk_nodes.mif + volume AI + compare/ --report on Clinical PDF + figure gallery --no-report off Skip PDFs --participants none participants.tsv (SOZ, group, covariates) --normative-model fit from controls Pre-fitted DK strength OLS pickle --control-group control Label of control rows in --participants

Legacy filenames dk_connectome.csv and connectome.csv are still discovered. Exit status 2 if no subjects are found; 1 on unsupported matrix shape.

docs.title: Analysis image (usual)
docs.text:
Standalone Apptainer/Singularity image that runs DK node strength, AI, volume AI, and clinical PDFs — the same job as dkt-ai-cohort. No repo checkout or Python env required.

oras://index.docker.io/phindagijimana321/nodestrength:0.1.0

Canonical file: nodestrength_0.1.0.sif. Build from this repo with bash containers/build.sh. Details: containers/README.md in GitHub.

docs.title: Apptainer
docs.text:
SIF=/path/to/nodestrength_0.1.0.sif
CONNECT=/path/to/connectomes     # one folder per subject
OUT=/path/to/results
FS=/path/to/freesurfer/subjects  # optional

apptainer run --cleanenv \
  -B "$CONNECT:$CONNECT:ro" \
  -B "$OUT:$OUT" \
  ${FS:+-B "$FS:$FS:ro"} \
  "$SIF" \
  "$CONNECT" "$OUT" ${FS:+"$FS"}

Or copy containers/run.sh beside the .sif:

./run.sh /path/to/connectomes /path/to/results
./run.sh /path/to/connectomes /path/to/results /path/to/freesurfer/subjects

Default: strength + volume + compare + PDF. --strength-only or --no-report skip pieces.

Per-subject inputs: dkt_connectome.csv (required), dk_nodes.mif (volume AI).

docs.title: Reconstruction image (optional)
docs.text:
A heavier Docker image (docker.io/phindagijimana321/nodestrength:latest in some lab notes) based on MRtrix3 with FreeSurfer/FSL/ANTs is for building connectomes (dwi2fod, tckgen, SIFT2, tck2connectome). If QSIPrep + QSIRecon already produced matrices, you do not need it.

docker pull phindagijimana321/nodestrength:latest
docker run --rm -v /path/to/data:/data \
    phindagijimana321/nodestrength:latest recon --help

See Pipeline details for the reconstruction recipe (Piper et al. 2026; MRtrix31).

docs.title: QSIPrep / QSIRecon instead
docs.text:
If your lab already runs QSIPrep + QSIRecon, point dkt-ai-cohort --root at the connectome directory. That is the recommended path for new BIDS datasets.

  1. Tournier J-D, Smith R, Raffelt D, et al. MRtrix3: A fast, flexible and open software framework for medical image reconstruction and visualisation. NeuroImage. 2019;202:116137. doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2019.116137 ↩

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: The analysis CLI is a Python package. Most users who already have connectome CSVs only need this install. Reconstruction (FOD, tractography, tck2connectome) is a separate problem: use QSIPrep + QSIRecon, or the analysis container if you already have dkt_connectome.csv files.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.9+ (3.12 recommended)
  • A POSIX environment (Linux or macOS). Windows: use WSL2.
  • Optional: Apptainer/Singularity or Docker for the standalone image
  • Optional: bctpy for the canonical Brain Connectivity Toolbox backend (otherwise a matching NumPy strengths_und is used)

docs.title: Python package
docs.text:
From a clone of the GitHub repository:

git clone https://github.com/phindagijimana/dwi-AI.git
cd dwi-AI
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[bct]"

Runtime dependencies (installed automatically): numpy, pandas, scipy, nibabel, reportlab, matplotlib, nilearn.

This registers three console scripts:

Command Module Typical use nodestrength nodestrength.cli:main Subcommand CLI (inspect, ingest, asymmetry, GLM, …) dkt-ai-cohort nodestrength.dk_cohort:main DK/DKT QSIRecon connectome folders dk-ai-cohort same Legacy alias

Confirm:

nodestrength --help
dkt-ai-cohort --help

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[bct]"    # bctpy — canonical strengths_und
pip install -e ".[viz]"    # VTK + ENIGMA Toolbox surfaces for report maps
pip install -e ".[dev]"    # pytest

Normative z-scores use a small OLS implementation (no statsmodels required). Mixed-design GLM (Pillai’s trace, partial η²) uses NumPy/SciPy in nodestrength.stats.

docs.title: What “success” looks like
docs.text:
• Matrix is square; 84×84 for fs_default DKT, or LUT length for Lausanne+THOMAS
  • Global strength is finite and > 0
  • Homologous pairs found (warnings list unpaired nodes)
  • side_ai in \([-1, 1]\) except log_ai
  • manifest.json lists warnings instead of dropping subjects silently

docs.title: Pipeline details
docs.text:
Two layers: reconstruction (optional container / QSIRecon) and analysis (this package).

flowchart TD
  subgraph recon [Reconstruction]
    T1[T1w] --> FS[FreeSurfer / HSVS]
    DWI[dMRI] --> PRE[denoise, unring, eddy/TOPUP]
    PRE --> FOD[dwi2fod msmt-csd]
    FS --> 5TT[5TT ACT]
    FOD --> TCK[tckgen iFOD2]
    5TT --> TCK
    TCK --> SIFT[tcksift2]
    FS --> LUT[parcellation]
    SIFT --> C[tck2connectome]
    LUT --> C
  end
  subgraph analysis [nodestrength]
    C --> STR[strengths_und]
    STR --> AI[laterality]
    AI --> Z[optional GAM z]
    Z --> GLM[optional mixed GLM]
  end

docs.title: Reconstruction (Piper-aligned)
docs.text:
Piper et al. 2026 used MRtrix3 multi-shell multi-tissue CSD, anatomically constrained tractography (ACT), and SIFT2. Canonical citations:

  • MRtrix3 framework — Tournier et al. 20191
  • MSMT-CSD — Jeurissen et al. 20142
  • ACT — Smith et al. 20123
  • SIFT2 — Smith et al. 20154
  • QSIPrep preprocessing — Cieslak et al. 20215

Default tckgen in the container: iFOD2, \(10^7\) streamlines (lab-configurable), ACT 5TT, backtrack. SIFT2 writes a per-streamline weight; tck2connectome -tck_weights_in sums weights between parcels.

Deterministic vs probabilistic

tckgen with Tensor_Det / FACT is not the same graph as iFOD2. Mixing them in one ROC table is a data error, not a statistics error. See Connectomics.

docs.title: Analysis mathematics
docs.text:
For undirected weighted adjacency \(W\):

\[ s_i = \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{w_{ij} + w_{ji}}{2} \]

This is BCT strengths_und6. Asymmetry for a homologous pair:

\[ \mathrm{AI} = \frac{s_L - s_R}{s_L + s_R} \]

Intrahemispheric strength zeroes edges that cross the midline before the sum. Volume AI substitutes parcel volume for \(s\).

Normative z-scores: residual of \(s_i\) after a GAM on controls (age, sex, motion, global strength), divided by control residual SD (Piper et al. 2026).

docs.title: Lausanne 2008 lookup tables (IDEAS)
docs.text:
Connectome row order is not FreeSurfer LUT order. Independent extraction from easy_lausanne GraphML (Cammoun et al. 20127) yields:

Scale Nodes (no brainstem) Hippocampus indices (L, R) 36 82 5, 12 60 128 5, 12 125 233 5, 12 250 462 5, 12

Order: drop Brain-Stem, then left subcortical, right subcortical, left DK cortex (split at finer scales), right DK cortex. Hippocampus remains a single node per hemisphere at every Lausanne 2008 scale.

If you use someone else’s CSV “LUT”, re-extract it. Matching node counts is not matching order.

docs.title: What this pipeline does not do
docs.text:
• Functional connectivity (Pearson/partial correlation, tangent space)
  • Network-based statistic (NBS) edgewise inference
  • Community detection / rich-club / graph spectra
  • Tractometry along bundles (AFQ, TractSeg)

Those are neighbouring methods; see Other connectomic methods and Graph theory beyond this tool.

Two entry points cover the common labs:

This page is the analogue of QSIPrep’s “Running” guide. Flags: CLI.

docs.title: Asymmetry indices
docs.text:
The brain is not symmetric. Structural and functional laterality have a long literature (Geschwind & Galaburda 19851; Toga & Thompson 20032; Kong et al. 2018 ENIGMA laterality of cortical thickness3; Guadalupe / ENIGMA laterality working group). In epilepsy, which hippocampus is smaller or less connected is often the clinical question.

This package turns a pair of homologous node strengths (or volumes) into laterality indices. Graph theory stops at \(s_L\) and \(s_R\); everything below is a contrast on that pair.

docs.title: Why laterality rather than \(s_L\) and \(s_R\) separately?
docs.text:
Raw strength is confounded by global reconstruction, brain size, and streamline count. A within-subject left-versus-right ratio cancels a large class of those confounds (any factor that multiplies both hemispheres). It does not cancel hemisphere-specific reconstruction bias (known gyral biases, B0 distortion that differs by side) — QC still matters.

Toga & Thompson (2003) review petalia, planum temporale, and volumetric asymmetries. Kong et al. (2018) show that cortical thickness laterality is reproducible at scale. Hippocampal volumetric asymmetry is a standard HS biomarker (Jack and subsequent epilepsy-MRI reviews). Connectivity AI is the same algebraic form on a different measurement.

docs.title: Side AI
docs.text:
For homologous values \(x_L, x_R\) (strength or volume):

\[ \mathrm{AI} = \frac{x_L - x_R}{x_L + x_R} \in [-1, 1] \]

Positive = left-dominant under this sign convention. When \(x_L+x_R=0\), AI is undefined (NaN), not 0 — a zero would look like perfect symmetry of two missing nodes.

Properties:

  • Scale-free: multiplying both sides by \(c>0\) does not change AI. That is why global streamline-count differences drop out.
  • Bounded: useful for mixed models and ROC.
  • Nonlinear near zero: a 10 vs 0 pair is \(\mathrm{AI}=1\), same as 10 000 vs 0.

A log-ratio

\[ \log\mathrm{AI} = \ln(x_L / x_R) \]

is unbounded and more sensitive when one side is near 0. We store log_ai alongside side_ai. It is undefined for non-positive values; those rows stay NaN.

Some papers use \((R-L)/(R+L)\) (right-minus-left). Always state the numerator. This CLI uses left-minus-right for side_ai.

docs.title: SOZ-aligned AI
docs.text:
If the seizure-onset zone side is known:

\[ \mathrm{AI_{SOZ}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{SOZ}} \cdot \mathrm{AI} \]

with a documented \(\sigma_{\mathrm{SOZ}}\) so that positive means ipsilateral stronger than contralateral (or the inverse — the CSV header / manifest.json is the contract). Bilateral or unknown SOZ cannot be aligned; those rows stay as side AI.

Piper et al. 20264 treat SOZ as a between-subject factor in a mixed GLM (nucleus × side × group/SOZ) rather than only a sign flip. Both are valid:

Approach Question Sign-flip AI “Is the SOZ side the weak side?” as one number per subject Mixed GLM with side × SOZ “Does the L/R pattern depend on which side is epileptic?”

--participants with a soz_side column enables the first; nodestrength analyze --within nucleus side --between group is the second.

docs.title: Volume AI
docs.text: Same formulae on parcel volume in mm³. In HS, volume AI is the classical imaging biomarker; connectivity AI is complementary. dkt-ai-cohort --with-volume-ai writes both and a compare table. Volume typically comes from dk_nodes.mif on the tractography grid (not always identical to FreeSurfer aseg volumes — another named choice).

docs.title: Intrahemispheric AI
docs.text:
Compute \(s_L, s_R\) from the intrahemispheric mask (Node strength), then AI. This is the IDEAS hippocampus default: contralateral projections (fornix/commissural reconstructions, callosal false positives) should not cancel a unilateral deficit.

dkt-ai-cohort always writes side_ai on whole-brain, intra, and inter strengths so you can see whether a laterality effect is driven by within-hemisphere wiring.

docs.title: Homologous pairing
docs.text: AI is only defined for paired nodes: Left-Hippocampus with Right-Hippocampus, lh.superiortemporal with rh.superiortemporal, THOMAS AV_L with AV_R. Midline structures (brainstem, some vermis labels) have no pair; they belong in a strength table, not an AI table. A LUT that orders left cortex then right cortex with a different split count will silently pair the wrong regions — the most dangerous bug in this analysis. Independent GraphML extraction is how this project checks Lausanne LUTs.

docs.title: ROC, sensitivity, specificity
docs.text:
To ask “does hippocampal AI separate left-HS from controls?” treat AI (or \(-AI\)) as a scalar classifier:

  1. ROC curve; AUC (Hanley & McNeil 1982). Correlated AUCs: DeLong et al. 19885.
  2. Pick an operating point → sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV.

Threshold choice changes sensitivity/specificity even when AUC is identical.

Rule Typical origin Notes Closest point to \((0,1)\) in ROC space common Python Euclidean in ROC coordinates, which are not equally scaled clinically Youden \(J=\mathrm{sens}+\mathrm{spec}-1\) Youden 19506 Maximises vertical distance from diagonal MATLAB perfcurve optrocpt Statistics Toolbox Not always closest-to-(0,1) pos_label inverted codebook Maps \(\mathrm{AUC}\mapsto 1-\mathrm{AUC}\)

If a MATLAB table used pos_label=0 for “Left HS”, sklearn with pos_label=1 inverts the curve. That is a label convention, not a different AI formula. Matching AUC to \(10^{-15}\) and still missing sens/spec almost always means a different operating point (optrocpt vs closest-to-corner). If you need MATLAB’s point, call MATLAB; do not “fix” the strength formula.

Prevalence matters for PPV/NPV; AUC does not know the clinic’s base rate.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Mixing det and prob Count in one ROC.
  • Mixing scales (L60 vs L250 hippocampus is the same biological structure but a different neighbourhood in \(W\)).
  • Treating MeanFA AI as Count AI.
  • Pairing unpaired nodes (brainstem) or the wrong LUT order.
  • Coding bilateral SOZ as left.
  • Reporting sensitivity without the threshold rule.

docs.title: Graph theory beyond this tool
docs.text:
The Brain Connectivity Toolbox (Rubinov & Sporns 2010)1 catalogues dozens of measures. MATLAB/Python BCT, NetworkX, bctpy, igraph, and Brainstorm implement most of them. This package uses one (strengths_und) plus laterality. The rest of the catalogue is real graph theory. This page is the map, with enough formula and literature that a newcomer can see what each measure is, what question it answers, and why we do not ship it by default.

Companion textbook: Fornito, Zalesky & Bullmore (2016)2. Companion primer: Graph theory primer.

docs.title: Clustering coefficient
docs.text: Question: are my neighbours connected to each other? Binary: \(C_i = 2t_i / k_i(k_i-1)\). Weighted: Onnela / Barrat / Zhang variants (name which). BCT: clustering_coef_bu, clustering_coef_wu. Pitfall: \(C\) rises automatically with density. Compare at matched density to a rewired null (van Wijk 20103). When to use: a segregation hypothesis (“the epileptic hippocampus is less locally clustered”), after you have stated the null.

docs.title: Local efficiency
docs.text: Question: if node \(i\) is removed, how well do its neighbours still communicate? Formula: global efficiency of the neighbourhood subgraph (Latora & Marchiori 20014; Achard & Bullmore 2007 on brain networks). BCT: efficiency_bin / efficiency_wei with local flag. Pitfall: needs a distance transform on weighted graphs; disconnected neighbourhoods drive the metric.

docs.title: Betweenness centrality
docs.text: Question: what fraction of shortest paths sit on \(i\)? Formula (Freeman 1977): \(b_i = \sum_{s\neq i \neq t} \sigma_{st}(i)/\sigma_{st}\). Weighted versions use a length matrix. BCT: betweenness_bin, betweenness_wei. Brandes (2001) algorithm is the practical implementation. Pitfall: a single bottleneck edge can dominate; very sensitive to false-positive long-range streamlines. Not a substitute for strength.

docs.title: Closeness and harmonic closeness
docs.text: Question: how near is \(i\) to everyone else? Closeness: \(1/\sum_j d_{ij}\) — undefined or awkward if the graph is disconnected. Harmonic: \(\sum_j 1/d_{ij}\) — well-defined with \(d_{ij}=\infty\). Pitfall: in a 400-node connectome almost everyone is 2–3 hops away; the dynamic range is tiny once density is high.

docs.title: Eigenvector, PageRank, Katz
docs.text: Question: is \(i\) connected to other well-connected nodes? Eigenvector: principal eigenvector of \(A\) (Bonacich 1987). PageRank: \((I-\alpha A D^{-1})^{-1}\) damped walk (Brin & Page 1998). Katz: walks of all lengths with attenuation \(\alpha\). BCT: eigenvector_centrality_und, pagerank_centrality. Pitfall: on undirected connected graphs these are highly correlated with strength. They earn their keep on directed or very heterogeneous graphs.

docs.title: Matching index
docs.text: Question: how similar are the neighbour sets of \(i\) and \(j\)? Used more as a generative term (Betzel et al. 20165) than as a clinical biomarker.

docs.title: Within-module degree \(z\) and participation \(P_i\)
docs.text: Question: provincial hub or connector hub? Requires a community partition first (Guimerà & Amaral 20056; Sporns, Honey & Kötter 2007). BCT: module_degree_zscore, participation_coef. Pitfall: garbage partition \(\Rightarrow\) garbage cartography. Run consensus communities, not one Louvain seed.

docs.title: Community detection
docs.text: Covered in the primer. Practical rule: report algorithm, resolution, consensus across runs, and \(Q\) versus a degree-preserving null. Leiden (Traag 2019)7 is the default upgrade from Louvain. Infomap (Rosvall & Bergstrom 2008) optimises a different objective (random-walk compression) and can disagree with \(Q\) — that disagreement is scientifically interesting, not a bug.

docs.title: Core–periphery and rich club
docs.text:
Borgatti & Everett (2000) formalise a dense core with a sparse periphery. The rich club \(\phi(k)\) (Colizza 2006; van den Heuvel & Sporns 20118) asks whether high-degree nodes are unexpectedly densely linked to each other. Hagmann et al. 2008’s “structural core” (posterior medial / parietal) is the empirical cousin.

Pitfall: \(\phi(k)\) must be normalised by a configuration-model null, \(\phi_{\mathrm{norm}}(k)=\phi(k)/\phi_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\). Raw \(\phi(k)\) always rises at high \(k\) in any heavy-tailed graph.

docs.title: Motifs and k-cores
docs.text:
Motifs: over-represented small subgraphs vs a null (Milo 2002; Sporns & Kötter 2004). Macroscale undirected connectomes have a limited motif zoo.

k-core: iteratively delete nodes with degree \(<k\). The remaining shell is a robust core (Alvarez-Hamelin; Hagmann-style cores). Cheap to compute; still needs a null if you compare groups.

docs.title: Global measures (one number per brain)
docs.text:
Measure Idea Canonical ref Main confound Characteristic path length \(L\) Mean shortest path Watts–Strogatz 1998 Density, disconnected nodes Global efficiency \(E_{\mathrm{glob}}\) Mean inverse path Latora & Marchiori 2001 Distance transform Small-world \(\sigma\), \(\omega\) High \(C\), short \(L\) vs nulls Humphries 2008; Telesford 2011 Almost always “significant” if null is ER Assortativity \(r\) Degree–degree correlation Newman 2002 Density, parcellation Modularity \(Q\) Quality of a partition Newman 2006 Resolution limit Synchronisability Laplacian spectrum Barahona & Pecora Model of dynamics, not a measurement Algebraic connectivity \(\lambda_2\) Fiedler value of \(L\) Fiedler 1973; Chung 1997 Component structure Graph energy / von Neumann entropy Spectral summaries — Hard to interpret clinically MST diameter, leaf fraction Stats on a tree backbone Stam 20149 Loses cycles on purpose

Global metrics are where forking paths explode: threshold × weight × atlas × null × metric. Button et al. (2013) on power and Ioannidis on false-positive science apply brutally here. A pre-registered strength+AI contrast is a more defensible paper than an uncorrected 50-metric BCT dump.

docs.title: Spectral methods in more detail
docs.text:
The Laplacian \(L=D-W\) (or the normalised version) is the adjacency matrix’s more structural cousin:

  • Connected components = dim ker \(L\).
  • Cheeger / Fiedler: a small \(\lambda_2\) means a sparse cut — the graph almost falls into two pieces. Spectral clustering uses the Fiedler vector as a 1-D embedding and thresholds it.
  • Graph signal processing: treat a cortical map (thickness, BOLD amplitude, an AI vector) as a signal on the nodes; the Laplacian eigenbasis is a Fourier basis on the connectome (Shuman 2013; Ortega 2018). Atasoy et al. (2016)10 called the structural eigenmaps connectome harmonics and related them to resting-state patterns.
  • Heat kernels / diffusion embedding: \(e^{-tL}\) is the graph analogue of a Gaussian blur; used in manifold learning on connectomes (Margulies 2016 “principal gradient” is a related embedding on functional connectivity).

Strength is \(\mathrm{diag}(D)\). If you only compute strength, you have not done spectral graph theory; you have done the degree sequence.

docs.title: Random-graph ensembles and statistical inference
docs.text:
Repeating the primer with the inference hat on:

  • Erdős–Rényi — too simple; destroys hubs.
  • Configuration model — preserves degrees; the default null for \(Q\), motifs, rich-club.
  • Stochastic block model — infers communities as a generative model (Peixoto’s graph-tool); comes with model selection (minimum description length) instead of a single \(Q\).
  • Exponential random graph models (ERGM) — specify \(P(G)\propto \exp(\theta\cdot \text{features})\). Poorly identified on \(n\sim 400\) MRI graphs; use with scepticism.
  • Geometric / hyperbolic / latent-space — nodes have coordinates; edges prefer short distances (Betzel 2016; Roberts, Perry, Lord et al.). The brain is spatially embedded; a null that ignores Euclidean distance will call every short-range triangle “clustering.”
  • Minimum spanning tree — one connected acyclic backbone; density is no longer a free parameter (Stam 2014). You lose all cycles, so clustering is identically zero; you study hierarchy of the tree instead.

Without some ensemble, “small-world” and “modular” are adjectives, not results (Fornito, Zalesky & Breakspear 201311).

docs.title: Directed, signed, temporal, higher-order
docs.text:
See the primer’s last technical section. Practical pointers:

  • Directed structural MRI is usually a mistake: tractography polarity is not axon polarity. Directed functional graphs are a different literature (DCM, Granger — Friston 2011).
  • Signed modularity must not treat a negative edge as “missing.” Rubinov & Sporns 2011 give the convention BCT uses.
  • Dynamic FC reliability is low at short windows (Noble, Scheinost & Constable; Laumann et al.). Do not compute 50 BCT metrics per window.
  • Higher-order / simplicial methods (Battiston 2020, 2021; Giusti, Ghrist, Bassett on clique topology) are active research. They are not a drop-in replacement for strengths_und.

docs.title: Why this package still only ships strength
docs.text:
Piper et al. 2026 asked whether thalamic nuclei differ in total structural coupling with cortex, by side and group12. That is a weighted-degree hypothesis. Efficiency, modularity, or rich-club would answer different questions and would require density-matched nulls the paper did not claim.

If you extend nodestrength with other BCT measures:

  1. Document the edge definition (Count vs FA vs SIFT2).
  2. Document the null.
  3. Pre-register the metric list.
  4. Do not Bonferroni 50 metrics on 288 subjects into a story.

The “connectomic garden of forking paths” is how the literature filled with unreplicable small-world papers. Strength plus a named laterality contrast is a narrower, cleaner claim.

docs.title: Connectomics
docs.text:
Connectomics is the project of mapping neural connections at a chosen scale (Sporns, Tononi & Kötter 20051; Lichtman & Sanes 2008 at microscale; Hagmann 2008 and the Human Connectome Project at macroscale23).

This tool lives at macroscale, in vivo, diffusion MRI. The matrix \(W\) that nodestrength consumes is not “the connectome” in the synaptic sense. It is a reconstruction. This page is how that reconstruction is made, why two labs’ \(W\) disagree, and which literatures sit next to it.

docs.title: Scales of connectomics (do not mix them)
docs.text:
Scale Object Methods Landmark Micro Synapses, neurites EM (White 1986 C. elegans; FlyEM; MICrONS) Lichtman & Sanes 2008 Meso Projection neurons, tracers Viral tracers, CLARITY, CoCoMac, Allen CCFv3 Markov et al. macaque; Oh et al. mouse Macro Grey-matter parcels, white-matter pathways dMRI tractography, polarised light, dissection Hagmann 2008; HCP

Jones, Knösche & Turner (2013)4 is the paper to read before treating a streamline count as an axon count.

docs.title: How a structural connectome is made
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  RAW[Raw dMRI] --> PRE[denoise, unring, eddy, TOPUP]
  PRE --> FOD[FOD / MSMT-CSD]
  T1[T1w] --> PARC[Parcellation]
  T1 --> ACT[5TT ACT]
  FOD --> TCK[tckgen]
  ACT --> TCK
  TCK --> FILT[SIFT2 / COMMIT]
  PARC --> C[tck2connectome]
  FILT --> C
  C --> W["W, the connectome"]
  1. Preprocess the diffusion data (motion, eddy, susceptibility). QSIPrep (Cieslak et al. 20215) is the current standard BIDS implementation.
  2. Estimate fibre orientations. DTI (Basser, Mattiello & LeBihan 1994) gives one ellipsoid per voxel — insufficient at crossings. HARDI / CSD (Tournier, Calamante & Connelly 2007) and MSMT-CSD (Jeurissen et al. 20146) give fibre orientation distributions (FODs) that can support multiple peaks.
  3. Grow streamlines. Deterministic: follow the peak (FACT, SD_STREAM). Probabilistic: sample the FOD (iFOD2 in MRtrix3). Anatomically constrained tractography (ACT; Smith et al. 20127) uses a 5-tissue-type image so streamlines terminate in grey matter rather than running into CSF.
  4. Filter. Raw tractograms over-represent easy paths. SIFT (Smith 20138) removes streamlines; SIFT2 (Smith 20159) keeps them all and assigns a weight so the FOD is explained. COMMIT (Daducci 201510) and LiFE (Pestilli 2014) are convex / biological alternatives.
  5. Parcellate and count. tck2connectome sums (weighted) streamlines between pairs of grey-matter labels.

MRtrix3 (Tournier et al. 201911) is the usual implementation of 2–5. QSIRecon wraps those recipes in BIDS.

docs.title: Deterministic vs probabilistic
docs.text:
Deterministic Probabilistic (iFOD2) Algorithm Follow the FOD peak Sample the FOD Typical \(W\) Sparser; weaker long-range Denser; more long-range False negatives Kissing / crossing missed Fewer misses False positives Fewer hallucinations Long-range invented connections Strength / AI Different numbers on the same subject Different numbers on the same subject

They are different experiments. A bitwise-identical Count matrix labelled both “det” and “prob” is a packaging error, not a replication. True deterministic Count on the same subjects is sparser and will move ROC AUC. IDEAS Figshare dumps have illustrated both the error (old “det” copied from prob) and the real difference (later true det zip).

docs.title: What tractography cannot promise
docs.text:
Read these before writing “we mapped the connectome”:

  • Jones, Knösche & Turner 2013 — fibre count and other fallacies4
  • Thomas et al. 2014, PNAS — anatomical accuracy is inherently limited12
  • Maier-Hein et al. 2017 — international tractography challenge; even experts disagree13
  • Schilling et al. 2019 — modern methods still limited14
  • Yeh et al. 2021 — challenges and opportunities review15
  • Reveley / Jbabdi / Calabrese — gyral bias, bottleneck issues, ground-truth animal comparisons

A zero in \(W\) means “this reconstruction did not draw a connection,” not “biology has no axons here.” A large \(w_{ij}\) means “many weighted streamlines ran between these parcels,” not “this is a strong synaptic projection.”

docs.title: Edge weights are different graphs
docs.text:
On the same tractogram you can write several matrices. They are not interchangeable biomarkers.

Weight How it is made What \(s_i=\sum_j w_{ij}\) then means Count Number of streamlines Raw reconstructed wiring mass; scales with tckgen count SIFT2-weighted count Streamline weights from SIFT2 Preferred quantitative structural edge (Smith 2015) CountScaled Count ÷ (volume and/or length) Attempts to correct parcel size; name the divisor Mean FA Average FA of voxels / streamlines on the path Mixes whether a path exists with microstructure of that path MD / RD / AD Same with other tensors Diffusivity load, not wiring mass Mean length Average streamline length Total millimetres of track, not connection weight

Gong et al. (2009)16 and Hagmann (2008) discuss weighted vs binary cortical networks. Never concatenate Count AI and MeanFA AI in one ROC without labelling the edge. In IDEAS-style trees you will see Count, CountScaled, MeanFA, MD, Length as separate experiments.

docs.title: Desikan–Killiany and fs_default
docs.text: Desikan et al. (2006)17: 34 cortical gyri per hemisphere from FreeSurfer aparc, plus subcortical aseg structures. MRtrix3 fs_default.txt is an 84-row lookup used by labelconvert. dkt-ai-cohort pairs homologous L/R labels on that grid. Thalamus is one node per side (Thalamus-Proper). Per-nucleus thalamus requires THOMAS (or similar) on top — that is the Piper atlas, not DK.

docs.title: Lausanne 2008 / Cammoun
docs.text: Hagmann 2008 and Cammoun et al. 201218: recursive subdivision of DK cortex. Published scales are approximately 36, 60, 125, 250 cortical parcels per hemisphere-style naming; after dropping brainstem and using both hemispheres plus subcortex, connectome sizes in easy_lausanne GraphML (this project) are 82 / 128 / 233 / 462 nodes. Hippocampus is not split. Row order is GraphML order: drop Brain-Stem, then left subcortical, right subcortical, left cortex, right cortex — not FreeSurferColorLUT.txt order. Matching node counts is not matching LUT.

docs.title: THOMAS thalamic nuclei
docs.text: Su et al., Thalamus Optimized Multi Atlas Segmentation19. Piper et al. 2026 merge THOMAS nuclei with cortical Lausanne/DK-style labels to ask which nucleus is under-connected20. Whole-thalamus DK AI cannot answer that.

docs.title: Other atlases you will meet
docs.text: AAL (Tzourio-Mazoyer 2002), Harvard-Oxford, Schaefer 201821, Glasser MMP 201622, Brainnetome (Fan 2016), AICHA, Yeo 7/17 (functional, not structural). Zalesky 2010: node choice changes every subsequent metric.

docs.title: Functional connectomics (not computed here)
docs.text:
Resting-state edges are typically Pearson or partial correlations of ROI time series (Biswal 1995; Smith et al. 201123). Confounds: motion (Power et al. 201224), global signal, atlas, pipeline (Ciric / Parkes “denoising” papers). Graph metrics can be computed on that matrix; thresholding and density are a literature of their own (van Wijk 201025). NBS (Zalesky, Fornito & Bullmore 201026) is the standard edgewise inference tool — see Other methods.

Do not run strengths_und on a Fisher-z matrix and interpret it as streamline strength.

docs.title: Epilepsy and the connectome
docs.text:
Focal epilepsy is a network disease as much as a focal lesion (Spencer 2002; Richardson 2012; Bernhardt, Bonilha & Gross 201527; Tavakol et al. 2019). Relevant strands:

  • Hippocampal sclerosis: volume loss and T2; laterality of volume is the classical MRI biomarker. Connectivity AI asks whether remaining tissue is also under-wired (Asymmetry).
  • Thalamocortical loops: absence and focal seizures both implicate thalamus; Piper et al. 2026 measure thalamocortical structural strength in children with focal epilepsy, with SOZ and mixed-design GLM20.
  • Graph metrics in epilepsy: reviews report altered clustering, efficiency, and hubs — with all the density caveats of the primer. This software does not add those metrics by default.
  • IDEAS I/II: Lausanne-scale structural connectomes used in this repository to apply strength+AI to hippocampus (Count/FA/Length, det vs prob, scales 36–250).

docs.title: Practical checklist before you score \(W\)
docs.text:
1. Named reconstruction (QSIPrep version, MRtrix3 version, iFOD2 vs FACT, SIFT2 on/off, streamline count).
  2. Named atlas, scale, LUT provenance.
  3. One weight type per contrast.
  4. Det and prob never pooled unlabeled.
  5. Diagonal zeroed, matrix square, symmetrised if undirected.
  6. Then — and only then — node strength.

docs.title: Graph theory primer
docs.text:
This page is a full vocabulary for reading network-neuroscience papers. It is not a substitute for Bondy & Murty, Diestel, or Newman’s Networks (2010)1, but it is meant to be enough that someone new to graphs can follow Rubinov & Sporns (2010)2, Fornito, Zalesky & Bullmore (2016)3, and then the rest of this site.

nodestrength uses one local weighted measure (strength) plus laterality. Everything else here is the field you are walking into. Measures this CLI does not compute are expanded again, with BCT names and pitfalls, on Graph theory beyond this tool.

docs.title: Why a graph at all?
docs.text:
A graph \(G=(V,E)\) is the simplest object that can say “these parts exist” (\(V\)) and “these pairs are related” (\(E\)). Euler’s Königsberg bridges (1736) already treated land masses as nodes and bridges as edges. In the 20th century the same object described social ties (Moreno; Granovetter 1973), citation networks, the web, and metabolic maps. Watts & Strogatz (1998)4 and Barabási & Albert (1999)5 made “complex networks” a discipline. Bullmore & Sporns (2009)6 brought that language to neuroimaging.

Three questions the object is for (Rubinov & Sporns 2010; Fornito et al. 2016):

  1. Integration — can this node reach, or be reached by, the rest of the system? Degree, strength, path length, efficiency, some centralities.
  2. Segregation — are there densely wired clusters? Clustering, transitivity, modules.
  3. Layout / economy — is the pattern small-world, core–periphery, hierarchical, spatially cheap? Watts–Strogatz; Bullmore & Sporns 2012 on the economical brain7; van den Heuvel & Sporns 2011 on the rich club8.

A hippocampal node-strength study is almost entirely question 1, plus left versus right. That is still graph theory, in the same way that measuring blood pressure is still cardiovascular physiology — a real but thin slice.

docs.title: Nodes, edges, simple graphs
docs.text:
• Node (vertex) \(i \in V\). In MRI, usually a grey-matter parcel. In microscopy, a neuron. In voxel graphs, a voxel.
  • Edge \(\{i,j\} \in E\) (undirected) or \((i,j) \in E\) (directed). In dMRI, a reconstructed white-matter connection. In fMRI, a statistical dependence.
  • Simple graph: no self-loops, at most one edge per pair. Connectomes are made simple by zeroing the diagonal \(w_{ii}=0\) (a parcel is not treated as connected to itself).
  • Order \(n = |V|\). Size \(m = |E|\).
  • Density (undirected, simple): \(2m / n(n-1)\). Density is the most important confound in brain-graph papers (van Wijk, Stam & Daffertshofer 201010). Two groups with different density will differ in almost every metric even if their organisation is the same.

docs.title: Directed, weighted, binary, multilayer
docs.text:
Adjective Meaning in MRI Typical use Undirected \(w_{ij}=w_{ji}\) after symmetrisation Structural connectomes (tck2connectome -symmetric) Directed Separate \(w_{ij}\) and \(w_{ji}\) Tractography can be written directed; axon polarity is not trusted. fMRI Granger/DCM are the directed literature (Friston 201111) Weighted \(w_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}_+\) Streamline count, SIFT2, mean FA, mean length Binary \(a_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) A thresholded skeleton; “is there a connection?” Signed \(w_{ij}\) may be negative Functional anticorrelations (Rubinov & Sporns 2011) Multilayer / multiplex several edge types on the same \(V\) Count and FA as layers (Kivelä et al. 201412; Boccaletti et al. 2014; Battiston et al. 2017, 2020)

The adjacency matrix \(A\) stores a binary graph; the weight matrix \(W\) stores a weighted one. Row \(i\) is “from \(i\)”. For undirected graphs \(W=W^\top\). Almost every BCT function is a recipe on \(A\) or \(W\).

Symmetrisation used here: replace \(W\) by \((W+W^\top)/2\). That is the undirected convention of strengths_und. If you skip it on an asymmetric tractography matrix, “strength” quietly becomes a mixture of in- and out-weight.

docs.title: Connected components
docs.text: A graph is connected if every node can reach every other by a path. dMRI connectomes at group-consistent thresholds are usually one giant component plus (sometimes) isolates. The number of connected components is the multiplicity of eigenvalue 0 of the Laplacian (see spectral section). Isolated nodes have strength 0; they must stay in the table so laterality can be undefined rather than silently 0.

docs.title: Degree and strength (this tool)
docs.text:
Degree of \(i\) is the number of neighbours:

\[ k_i = \sum_{j \neq i} a_{ij} \]

On a directed graph one splits in-degree \(k_i^{\mathrm{in}}=\sum_j a_{ji}\) and out-degree \(k_i^{\mathrm{out}}=\sum_j a_{ij}\).

Strength is the weighted analogue (Barrat, Barthélemy, Pastor-Satorras & Vespignani 200413; Opsahl, Agneessens & Skvoretz 201014; Rubinov & Sporns 2010):

\[ s_i = \sum_{j \neq i} w_{ij} \]

BCT name: strengths_und (undirected) or strengths_dir (in/out). That is the entire computational core of this repository. High strength means “this parcel participates in a large total weight of reconstructed connections.” It does not mean “this parcel is a topological hub.” Hubs combine how much connection mass with where those edges go (betweenness, participation, rich-club membership; Sporns, Honey & Kötter 200715; van den Heuvel & Sporns 2011, 201389).

Opsahl et al. (2010) generalise node centrality as a tunable mix of degree and strength, \(k_i \times (s_i/k_i)^\alpha\). BCT strengths_und is the \(\alpha=1\) end: pure weight sum. See Node strength for biology, intrahemispheric masks, and normalisation.

Degree / strength distribution \(P(k)\) or \(P(s)\) is the first global fingerprint of a network. Report the empirical histogram. Do not assume it is a power law (next section but one).

docs.title: Paths, distance, and efficiency
docs.text:
A walk is a sequence of edges. A trail does not repeat edges. A path does not repeat nodes. The shortest-path length \(d_{ij}\) is the fewest hops (binary) or the smallest sum of distances (weighted).

On a weighted brain graph, a large \(w_{ij}\) should mean a short distance, so one almost always transforms weights before running Dijkstra / Floyd–Warshall:

\[ \ell_{ij} = \frac{1}{w_{ij}} \quad \text{or} \quad \ell_{ij} = -\log w_{ij} \]

(Rubinov & Sporns 2010). Using raw streamline counts as distances would make strong connections look far. BCT distance_wei implements the inverse-weight convention unless you pass a custom length matrix.

Characteristic path length of a connected graph:

\[ L = \frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i \neq j} d_{ij} \]

Global efficiency (Latora & Marchiori 200116) is the mean inverse distance, and remains defined if the graph is disconnected (\(d_{ij}=\infty \Rightarrow 1/d_{ij}=0\)):

\[ E_{\mathrm{glob}} = \frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i \neq j} \frac{1}{d_{ij}} \]

Local efficiency of node \(i\) is the global efficiency of the subgraph induced by \(i\)’s neighbours (how well they communicate if \(i\) is removed). That is a segregation-plus-fault-tolerance measure, not a first-order sum.

nodestrength computes none of these. If you add them, you need a distance transform, a density-matched null, and a statement about disconnected nodes.

docs.title: Binary clustering
docs.text:
The local clustering coefficient of \(i\) is the fraction of pairs among \(i\)’s neighbours that are themselves connected (Watts & Strogatz 19984):

\[ C_i = \frac{2 t_i}{k_i(k_i-1)} \]

where \(t_i\) is the number of triangles through \(i\). Average \(C = n^{-1}\sum_i C_i\). Transitivity is a related global ratio \(3\times\text{triangles}/\text{connected triples}\) that does not overweight low-degree nodes (Newman). High clustering = local triangles = segregation.

docs.title: Weighted clustering
docs.text:
Several generalisations exist and they are not interchangeable:

  • Barrat et al. 2004 — weights on the two edges from \(i\) to its neighbours.
  • Onnela et al. 200517 — geometric mean of the three edge weights of each triangle (BCT clustering_coef_wu uses this family).
  • Zhang & Horvath / other variants.

Always name which formula you used. Clustering on a dense probabilistic connectome is not comparable to clustering on a sparse deterministic one without a null at the same density (van Wijk 201010; Fornito, Zalesky & Breakspear 201341).

docs.title: Motifs
docs.text: A motif is a small recurrent subgraph (Milo et al. 200218). In directed neuronal / C. elegans / macaque networks, specific 3-node motifs are over-represented (Sporns & Kötter 200419). Macroscale undirected dMRI graphs have fewer interesting 3-node types (a triangle or not). Motif analysis needs a degree-preserving null; otherwise “we found triangles” is just “the graph is clustered.”

docs.title: Community detection and modularity
docs.text:
Brain networks are modular: nodes fall into communities with dense internal edges and sparser edges between communities (Meunier, Lambiotte & Bullmore 201020; Sporns & Betzel 2016).

Newman’s modularity \(Q\) (Newman 200621; Newman & Girvan 2004) scores a partition \(\{c_i\}\):

\[ Q = \frac{1}{2m}\sum_{ij}\left(A_{ij}-\frac{k_i k_j}{2m}\right)\delta(c_i,c_j) \]

The term \(k_i k_j / 2m\) is the expected edge weight in a random graph with the same degrees (the configuration-model null). Weighted and directed generalisations exist (Leicht & Newman 2008; Rubinov & Sporns 2011).

Algorithms (none of these are in nodestrength):

Algorithm Idea Refs Newman spectral / greedy Maximise \(Q\) Newman 2006 Louvain Multilevel greedy Blondel et al. 200822 Leiden Louvain fix (connected communities) Traag, Waltman & van Eck 201923 Infomap Compress random-walk description length Rosvall & Bergstrom 200824 Stochastic block model Generate edges from group labels Peixoto; Karrer & Newman 2011

Resolution limit (Fortunato & Barthélemy 200725): \(Q\) cannot see communities smaller than a scale set by \(m\). Multiresolution Potts / Reichardt–Bornholdt models and the SBM are the usual responses. Never treat a single Louvain run as the modules of the brain; consensus clustering across resolutions is the honest report (Lancichinetti & Fortunato 2009, 201226).

Once you have a partition, two node measures become available:

  • Within-module degree z-score — is \(i\) a hub inside its module?
  • Participation coefficient \(P_i\) (Guimerà & Amaral 200527) — are \(i\)’s edges spread across modules or concentrated in one?

Provincial hubs: high \(z\), low \(P\). Connector hubs: high \(P\). This is the cartographic classification used in many hub papers (Sporns 2007; van den Heuvel & Sporns 2013). Strength alone cannot draw that map.

docs.title: Small-world
docs.text:
Watts & Strogatz (1998) interpolates a ring lattice (high \(C\), long paths) toward a random graph (low \(C\), short paths). In the middle: high clustering and short paths — a small world.

Humphries & Gurney (2008)28 summarise this as

\[ \sigma = \frac{C/C_{\mathrm{rand}}}{L/L_{\mathrm{rand}}} \]

with \(\sigma>1\) called small-world. Telesford et al. (2011)29 prefer

\[ \omega = \frac{L_{\mathrm{rand}}}{L} - \frac{C}{C_{\mathrm{latt}}} \]

near 0 for small-world. Bassett & Bullmore (2006, 2017)3031 review the brain literature and the caveats: \(\sigma\) is almost always \(>1\) on thresholded MRI graphs because density and lattice nulls are poorly specified. A small-world claim requires an explicit null, matched density, and preferably \(\omega\) or a generative model (Betzel et al. 201632), not a \(\sigma\) table.

docs.title: Scale-free
docs.text: Barabási & Albert (1999)5: growth plus preferential attachment \(\Rightarrow P(k)\sim k^{-\gamma}\). Many early brain papers reported “scale-free connectomes.” Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009)33 showed how to test power laws properly (KS, xmin, alternative distributions). Broido & Clauset (2019)34 conclude that scale-free networks are rare. Structural MRI degree distributions are typically broad-tailed, not pure power laws. Report \(P(s)\) and a fitted alternative (log-normal, truncated power law). Do not write “scale-free” because a log–log plot looked straight.

docs.title: The centrality family
docs.text:
“Centrality” is not one number. It is a family of answers to “which nodes matter?” (Freeman 1978; Borgatti 2005).

Measure Formula / idea BCT-style name What it asks Degree / strength \(k_i\) or \(s_i\) degrees_und / strengths_und How much connection mass? Betweenness fraction of shortest paths through \(i\) betweenness_bin / _wei Does traffic sit on this node? Freeman 197735 Closeness \(1/\sum_j d_{ij}\) closeness_bin How near to all others? Harmonic closeness \(\sum_j 1/d_{ij}\) — Like closeness, defined if disconnected Eigenvector \(Ax=\lambda x\), leading \(x\) eigenvector_centrality_und Connected to other well-connected nodes? Bonacich 1987 PageRank damped random walk pagerank_centrality Brin & Page 1998 Katz \((I-\alpha A)^{-1}\) — Walks of all lengths Participation diversity of modules participation_coef Guimerà & Amaral 2005 Flow / current-flow betweenness electrical analogue — Newman; Brandes & Fleischer

Rich-club coefficient \(\phi(k)\) (Colizza et al. 2006; Opsahl 2008; van den Heuvel & Sporns 20118): among nodes with degree \(>k\), what fraction of possible edges exist, relative to a degree-preserving null? A rich club is a densely linked hub core — the “structural core” of Hagmann 2008 by another name. Strength does not tell you whether a strong hippocampus sits in that core.

Only the first row is implemented in this package.

docs.title: Assortativity and mixing
docs.text:
Assortativity \(r\) (Newman 2002, 200336) is the Pearson correlation of the degrees (or strengths) of nodes at two ends of an edge. Social networks are assortative (hubs link to hubs); many technological graphs are disassortative. Brain structural networks are often reported as assortative, consistent with a rich club, but the coefficient is density- and parcellation-sensitive.

Related: matching index (similarity of two nodes’ neighbour sets) — used as a generative-model term (Betzel 2016) more than as a biomarker.

docs.title: Null models (why a number is not a finding)
docs.text:
A network metric without a null is not evidence of organisation (Fornito, Zalesky & Breakspear 201341). Common ensembles:

Null What it preserves Use Erdős–Rényi \(G(n,p)\) or \(G(n,m)\) \(n\), density Too weak for brain graphs (destroys degree sequence) Configuration model / Maslov–Sneppen rewiring Degree sequence Maslov & Sneppen 200237; standard for \(Q\), \(\phi(k)\), motifs Weight-preserving rewiring Strengths / weights Weighted clustering, efficiency Lattice Spatial neighbours Small-world \(\omega\) Spatially embedded / geometric Distance distribution Roberts et al.; Betzel; the brain is a physical object (Bullmore & Sporns 2012) Minimum spanning tree A loop-free backbone Stam et al. 201438; avoids density by construction Stochastic block model Community labels Inference, not only a null

nodestrength does not run nulls. Strength and AI against a clinical control group are using a biological null (patients vs controls), which is a different and valid question. What you must not do is compute clustering on patients vs controls at different densities and call it “altered small-worldness.”

docs.title: Spectral graph theory (the linear-algebra half)
docs.text:
Let \(D=\mathrm{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\) be the strength matrix. The combinatorial Laplacian is

\[ L = D - W \]

Facts used constantly (Chung 1997; Spielman; Newman):

  • \(L\mathbf{1}=0\). Multiplicity of eigenvalue 0 = number of connected components.
  • The Fiedler value \(\lambda_2\) (algebraic connectivity) is small when the graph has a weak cut. Cheeger’s inequality relates \(\lambda_2\) to the sparsest cut.
  • The normalised Laplacian \(D^{-1/2} L D^{-1/2}\) is the basis of spectral clustering (Shi & Malik; Ng, Jordan & Weiss).
  • Connectome harmonics (Atasoy, Donnelly & Pearson 201639) are the eigenvectors of \(L\) on a structural connectome, used as a basis for cortical activity — graph signal processing on the brain (Shuman et al. 2013; Huang et al.; Ortega et al. 2018).

Strength is the diagonal of \(D\): the zeroth spectral object. Eigenvector centrality, harmonics, and cuts all live in the rest of the spectrum. That is “graph theory” in the course-catalogue sense, and it is out of scope for the CLI.

docs.title: Directed, signed, temporal, higher-order
docs.text:
Macroscale streamline connectomes are usually treated as undirected, positive, static, pairwise. The rest of graph theory is a cube of generalisations (Battiston et al. 2020, 202140):

  • Directed: in-/out-strength, reciprocity, trophic levels, cycle space.
  • Signed: positive and negative edges (functional anticorrelations); requires signed-modularity conventions (Rubinov & Sporns 2011).
  • Temporal / time-respecting paths: Holme & Saramäki 2012; dynamic FC sliding windows (Lurie et al. 2020 — with strong caveats from Laumann, Noble, and others on reliability).
  • Higher-order: hypergraphs, simplicial complexes, motif-based simplices, O-information (Rosas et al.). A triangle is no longer just clustering; it is a 2-simplex.

If a paper says “we applied graph theory to the connectome,” ask which quadrant of that cube, which null, and which edge definition.

docs.title: What MRI papers get wrong (a short list)
docs.text:
Drawn from Fornito, Zalesky & Breakspear (2013)41, van Wijk et al. (2010)10, de Reus & van den Heuvel (2013), and Jones, Knösche & Turner (2013):

  1. Thresholding two groups to the same density vs the same weight cutoff answers different questions; say which.
  2. Comparing 84-node DK graphs to 1000-node Schaefer graphs as if \(C\) and \(E\) were intensive quantities.
  3. Calling streamline count an axon count.
  4. Reporting 40 BCT metrics × 4 scales with uncorrected \(p\).
  5. “Small-world” or “scale-free” as a default adjective.
  6. Treating a correlation matrix like a structural adjacency (zeros, negatives, and nulls all differ).

The honest minimal report for this tool is: atlas, scale, LUT order, reconstruction (det/prob, SIFT2 or not), edge weight, intra- vs whole-brain strength, AI formula, and the clinical contrast. That is already a lot. Adding clustering does not make it “more graph theory”; it makes it a different paper.

docs.title: Why represent the brain as a network?
docs.text:
The short answer: because we want a language for parts, connections, and the pattern of those connections, not only for the size or intensity of a single region.

A mass-univariate voxel test can say “this hippocampus is small.” It cannot say “this hippocampus is weakly wired to ipsilateral temporal cortex, and that wiring pattern is more diagnostic than volume.” Network neuroscience exists for the second sentence.

In this field a node is a parcel of grey matter (or a neuron, a voxel, a recording site). An edge is a measured relationship — streamlines of white matter, a statistical dependence in BOLD, a synaptic count from tracers or electron microscopy. The object of study is the graph \(G=(V,E)\), often weighted. Agenda-setting reviews: Bullmore & Sporns (2009)1, Rubinov & Sporns (2010)2, Fornito, Zalesky & Bullmore (2016)3, Bassett & Sporns (2017)4.

docs.title: A short history of the idea
docs.text:
Year What happened Ref 19th–20th c. Golgi, Cajal, the neuron doctrine; the brain is already a network of cells — 1991– Macroscopic “connectome” language; Crick & Jones call for a human brain map Crick & Jones 1993 2005 Sporns, Tononi & Kötter name the human connectome as a structural description Sporns 20055 2005–2008 First diffusion-MRI cortical networks Hagmann 2005, 20086; Iturria-Medina; Gong 2009 2009 Nature Reviews Neuroscience review makes graph metrics standard vocabulary Bullmore & Sporns 2009 2010 BCT paper: a shared catalogue of measures (including strength) Rubinov & Sporns 2010 2010–2013 HCP; warnings about nodes, density, pitfalls Van Essen 20137; Zalesky 2010; Fornito 2013 2017– “Network neuroscience” as a named field Bassett & Sporns 2017

Microscale connectomics (Lichtman & Sanes 2008; C. elegans White et al. 1986; FlyEM, MICrONS) uses the same word at a different scale: synapses, not streamlines. Do not mix those literatures in one methods sentence.

docs.title: Three questions the graph is for
docs.text:
1. Integration. Can this region talk to the rest of the brain? Degree / strength — the quantity nodestrength computes — is the first-order answer. Path length and efficiency are higher-order answers (how indirectly it talks).
  2. Segregation. Are there clusters that are densely wired internally and sparsely wired between? Clustering, transitivity, modularity, communities (Meunier, Lambiotte & Bullmore 2010).
  3. Layout / economy. Is the wiring cheap, small-world, core–periphery, hierarchical? Watts–Strogatz (1998)8; Barabási–Albert (1999)9 (use critically); Bullmore & Sporns (2012) on the economical brain10; Bassett & Bullmore (2017) on small-world brain networks11; van den Heuvel & Sporns (2011) on the rich club.

A hippocampal node-strength study is almost entirely question 1, plus laterality. It is still graph theory. It is not “the” graph-theory paper; it does not need to be.

docs.title: Structural vs functional vs effective connectivity
docs.text:
Friston (2011)12 is the canonical trichotomy.

Kind Typical measurement Edge meaning What a zero means Canonical refs Structural dMRI tractography; tracers (CoCoMac, Allen) Anatomical pathway “We did not reconstruct a connection” — not “no axons exist” Hagmann 2008; Sporns 2005; Markov et al. macaque Functional fMRI / EEG / MEG correlations Statistical dependence “Time series are uncorrelated under this model” Biswal 199513; Smith 2011 Effective DCM, some Granger, perturb-and-measure Directed causal influence Model-dependent Friston 2003, 2011

nodestrength is structural. Do not treat a Count matrix as if it were a Pearson matrix: the null models, the meaning of a zero, the role of negative weights, and the statistics all differ (Zalesky 2010 on node choice14; Fornito, Zalesky & Breakspear 2013 on pitfalls15). Running strengths_und on Fisher-z functional connectivity is mathematically defined and biologically a different construct — call it “weighted functional degree,” not “streamline strength.”

docs.title: Why parcellate?
docs.text:
A voxel-wise white-matter graph has \(\sim 10^5\)–\(10^6\) nodes and is dominated by noise and spatial autocorrelation. Atlases trade spatial detail for stable, named nodes:

  • Desikan–Killiany (Desikan 2006)16 — gyral, ~34 cortical regions per hemisphere; this package’s fs_default / DKT path.
  • Destrieux — finer gyral/sulcal.
  • AAL (Tzourio-Mazoyer 2002) — still common, not recommended as a first choice.
  • Lausanne / Cammoun 201217 — recursive splits of DK; scales ~36/60/125/250. IDEAS connectomes in this project.
  • Schaefer 2018 — gradient-informed functional parcels at 100–1000 nodes.
  • Glasser MMP 2016 — multi-modal HCP parcels (360 cortical).
  • Brainnetome (Fan 2016) — structural–functional hybrid, includes subcortical.

Changing the atlas changes the graph (Zalesky et al. 201014; de Reus & van den Heuvel 201318). There is no such thing as “the” clustering coefficient of a subject — only \(C\) for a named atlas, scale, threshold, and weight. Always report:

  1. Atlas name and version
  2. Scale / node count
  3. Row order (LUT) — matching \(n\) is not matching order
  4. Whether brainstem / white-matter / cerebellum nodes were dropped

Lausanne 2008 hippocampus is one node per hemisphere at every scale. Finer scales split neocortex, not the hippocampus. That fact matters for IDEAS hippocampal AI.

docs.title: The brain as an economical network
docs.text: Wiring costs energy and volume. Bullmore & Sporns (2012)10 review the tension between cost (prefer short fibres) and topological value (a few long fibres, a rich club, to keep paths short). Generative models that grow edges from spatial distance plus homophily can reproduce many connectome statistics (Betzel et al. 2016; Vértes et al. 2012 for functional graphs). If your “clustering” is exactly what a distance-preserving null predicts, you have rediscovered that nearby cortex is more often connected — anatomy, not a new organisation.

docs.title: Other methods in connectomics
docs.text:
Node strength is one local summary of one kind of matrix. The field is larger. This page maps neighbouring methods you will see in papers, what question each answers, key citations, and whether this repository implements them (almost never).

If your question is “is this region under-connected in total?”, stay on node strength. If your question is any of the rows below, you need a different tool — not a different flag on dkt-ai-cohort.

docs.title: Network-based statistic (NBS)
docs.text:
Zalesky, Fornito & Bullmore (2010)1. Procedure:

  1. Mass-univariate test on each edge (t-test, GLM).
  2. Threshold edges at an uncorrected primary \(t\).
  3. Find connected components of supra-threshold edges.
  4. Permute group labels; the null is the size (or intensity) of the largest component.

Family-wise error is controlled at the component level, not the edge level. Use when the hypothesis is “some connections differ,” not “this node’s total wiring differs.” Strength can be significant while NBS is not (a distributed weak degree effect) and vice versa (a focal bundle).

Related: TFNBS (Baggio), MFC / “threshold-free” variants, FDR on edges (more conservative, no spatial clustering).

docs.title: Connectome-based predictive modelling (CPM)
docs.text: Shen et al. (2017)2: correlate every edge with a behaviour, keep positively/negatively associated edges, sum them, fit a linear model, cross-validate. A prediction method, not a graph-theory method. Requires honest cross-validation (no leaking the edge mask).

docs.title: MDMR, graphical lasso, tangent space
docs.text: Multivariate distance matrix regression (McArtor / Shehzad-style neuroimaging uses): is the pattern of connectivity different? Graphical lasso (Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani): sparse inverse covariance as an “effective” functional graph. Tangent-space embedding of covariance matrices (Varoquaux, Poldrack’s work, Nilearn): the right geometry for classifying functional connectomes. All of this is fMRI-adjacent; do not apply graphical lasso to a streamline Count matrix and call it SIFT.

docs.title: Bundle- and voxel-level white matter
docs.text:
These are not connectomes. They keep anatomy that node strength throws away.

Method Object What you get Landmark DTI voxel maps FA, MD, RD per voxel Microstructure, crossings unresolved Basser 1994 TBSS FA skeleton Voxelwise group FA Smith 20063 Tractometry / AFQ Named bundle, points along it FA/MD profile of e.g. uncinate Yeatman 20124 TractSeg CNN bundle mask 72+ bundles without a full connectome Wasserthal 2018 Apparent fibre density CSD intra-axonal density Per-direction density Raffelt 2012 Fixel-based analysis Fibre-bundle element FD, FC, FDC at crossings Raffelt 2015, 20175

Piper-style node strength collapses every bundle that touches a parcel into one number. If the scientific claim is “the fornix is degenerated,” use AFQ/FBA/TractSeg, not strengths_und of the hippocampus.

docs.title: Microstructure-informed tractography (changing \(W\) before strength)
docs.text:
These methods sit upstream of this CLI. They change the numbers in \(W\).

Method Idea Ref SIFT Delete streamlines until FODs are explained Smith 2013 SIFT2 Keep streamlines; fit a weight per streamline Smith 20156 COMMIT Convex fit of microstructural contributions Daducci 20157 LiFE Linear fascicle evaluation vs a forward model Pestilli 2014 Global tractography Jointly fit all tracks Reisert 2011; Christiaens 2015

If two labs disagree on hippocampal AI, the first question is not OLS vs GAM; it is whether SIFT2 was on and whether det vs prob was labelled.

docs.title: Functional and effective connectivity
docs.text:
Covered as a trichotomy in Why graphs. Methods you will see:

  • Pearson / partial correlation of ROI time series (Biswal 1995; Smith 2011).
  • ICA / canonical ICA (Calhoun; Smith HCP ICA).
  • DCM (Friston 2003, 20118) — generative, directed, model comparison with free energy.
  • Granger causality on fMRI: sampling-rate and haemodynamic caveats are severe.
  • MEG/EEG amplitude-envelope coupling (Hipp 2012); phase-locking; wPLI.

You can compute strength on a correlation matrix. Interpret it as weighted functional degree, cite the functional pipeline, and use an appropriate null (often a correlation-preserving or phase-randomised one, not Maslov–Sneppen on a binary skeleton).

docs.title: Multi-layer, temporal, morphometric, covariance
docs.text:
• Multilayer / multiplex (Kivelä 2014; Battiston; Vaiana & Muldoon): structural layer + functional layer on the same nodes; intra- and inter-layer edges. Participation across layers is a new measure.
  • Dynamic FC: sliding windows (Hutchison; Calhoun; Lurie 2020 review). Reliability at short windows is poor (Noble; Laumann).
  • Morphometric similarity networks (Seidlitz et al. 20189): edges from similarity of multivariate morphology (thickness, myelination, …). Not axons.
  • Structural covariance of thickness (Mechelli; Alexander-Bloch): group-level correlation of anatomy across subjects. A different object from a single-subject dMRI graph; do not compare \(C\) of a covariance network to \(C\) of a tractogram.

docs.title: Machine learning on connectomes
docs.text:
• BrainNetCNN (Kawahara 2017) — edge-to-edge, edge-to-node filters on \(W\).
  • Graph neural nets on brain graphs — large, fast-moving review literature; data-hungry; easy to overfit 288 subjects.
  • Kernel two-sample tests (MMD) on graphs.
  • Harmonisation: ComBat-style empirical Bayes for connectivity (Fortin; Pomponio; neuroCombat). Scanner effects will otherwise look like group effects.

nodestrength stops at features (strength, AI, z). The only classifier it supports is optional ROC on a single AI column.

docs.title: Spatial statistics on the surface (not graphs)
docs.text: GLM on thickness, myelination, or an AI map (FreeSurfer; HCP pipelines). PALM permutation inference (Winkler 201410) with exchangeability blocks. A hippocampal volume effect and a hippocampal strength effect can coexist; they are not two graph metrics, they are two modalities.
